The Dynamic Spill-Up Algorithm

The crown jewel of the Context Bubble is its Dynamic Spill-Up Engine:

  1. Surplus Release: During prompt compilation, every allotment builder runs. If an allotment (like context_files) uses less than its allocated budget (or returns empty), its unused token share is immediately released into a shared donor pool.
  2. Rank-Ordered Claims: Over-budget allotments claim the surplus in strict priority order (Rank 1 policy claims first, followed by Rank 2, 3, etc.).
  3. Even Donor Draw: Claimants do not steal greedily from one source; they draw evenly across all donor allotments.
  4. Elastic Rebound: The moment a donor allotment needs its tokens back on a subsequent turn (e.g. the user uploads a large file), the donor reclaims its baseline, and the claimant shrinks back gracefully.
  5. Defensive Truncation: If an allotment still exceeds its expanded grant, it truncates safely based on its keep policy (keep="end" retains the latest chat turns; keep="start" preserves foundational policy rules).

Dual-Tier Chunked-104a Persistence & Anti-Spoofing

Context bubbles don't live as ephemeral RAM strings. Every allotment is chunked into <context_dir>/bubble/allotments/<name>.104a.bejson using the frozen Core chunking engine. Then, the entire bubble directory is packaged into Context_Bubble.104a.bejson with SHA-256 integrity verification at both layers.

Furthermore, the engine includes built-in security defanging: if an adversary injects prompt injection tokens like [END CONTEXT BUBBLE] into a document or user message, the bubble parser neutralizes the delimiter before compilation, preventing context breakout attacks.

Why the Interactions API Destroys Classic Chat Endpoints

Traditional chat completions (like generateContent or OpenAI /v1/chat/completions) are stateless. Every single turn, your client has to re-upload the entire conversation history, re-chunk the prompt, and pay full price for context tokens. The Gemini Interactions API introduces server-side state chaining via previous_interaction_id: the model maintains the conversation bubble on Google's TPU clusters, slashing token bandwidth and latency for multi-turn agentic workflows.

The 5 Golden Wire Rules (Hardened Against API Traps)

Google's Interactions API has undocumented failure modes that trip up almost every SDK. Subsystem 3 embeds strict architectural defenses against each one:

  1. Header Authentication Invariant: The client sends x-goog-api-key: <key> in HTTP headers. Passing ?key= in the query string is rejected or leaks secrets in proxy access logs.
  2. Incident 7 (The generation_config Poison Pill): In standard Gemini endpoints, you pass generation_config for temperature and max tokens. On the Interactions API, passing generation_config causes the API to silently drop or break the call! Subsystem 3 strips this field by default, ensuring uninterrupted turn completion.
  3. Incident 5 (Attachment Wire Formatting):
    • Text & Code: Transmitted as raw text ({"type": "text", "text": "..."}) — zero base64 encoding bloat!
    • Images: Transmitted as {"type": "image", "data": "<base64>", "mime_type": "..."}.
    • Documents (PDF/Binary): Transmitted as {"type": "document", "data": "<base64>", "mime_type": "..."}.
    • Prohibited: inline_data belongs to the legacy API and silently drops files on the Interactions endpoint.
  4. Function Call & Step Traversal: Responses return steps inside the "steps" array (never "outputs"). Tool arguments arrive strictly under the "arguments" key (never "args").
  5. Function Result Enclosure: When returning tool execution results, the "result" field must be an array of content objects ([{"type": "text", "text": "..."}]). Returning a bare dictionary causes immediate HTTP 400 rejection.

Crash Recovery & Transaction Journaling

Concurrency and power outages are solved at the filesystem level. The brain engine enforces PID-locked serialization via brain_state/brain.lock. Every batch modification is staged into brain_state/txn/, executed, and deep-verified (mfdb_core_deep_verify). If the host script crashes or power is lost mid-write, the startup recovery hook detects the uncommitted batch on next launch, rolls back to the clean snapshot, and resumes without losing a single byte of database integrity.
